title: Two paralyzed BrainGate2 participants type on a two-handed QWERTY keyboard through an intracortical neuroprosthesis, and one reaches 22 words per minute at 1.6% word error
summary: A BrainGate2 implant with a recurrent neural network decoder turned two paralyzed men's attempted finger movements into typing, at up to 22 words per minute with a 1.6% word error rate.
account: T17 and T18 took part in the BrainGate2 pilot trial (NCT00912041). T17 is a 33-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, tetraplegia and anarthria. He depends on a ventilator. T18 is a 48-year-old man who had a cervical spinal cord injury, graded C4 ASIA A, about 18 months before enrollment. Each received six 64-electrode Utah arrays in precentral gyrus. A decoder of five gated recurrent unit layers, with a 5-gram language model, turned attempted finger movements into QWERTY keystrokes. It needed as few as 30 calibration sentences. Research sessions took place at each participant's place of residence, on trial days 44 to 144. T18 reached 110 characters (22 words) per minute with a 1.6% word error rate. T17 reached 47 characters per minute. Both typed sentences of their own choosing. The paper describes independent use as future work. The work was published in Nature Neuroscience on 16 March 2026. On 30 March 2026 the same team reported in Cell Reports that decoding of attempted speech in T17 was not accurate enough for effective communication. The authors write that they provided communication to T17 through the QWERTY typing interface.
purpose: The typing neuroprosthesis was built to restore communication for people with paralysis. It decodes attempted finger movements into keystrokes. The typing the two participants achieved is exactly that purpose.
system: BrainGate2 intracortical typing neuroprosthesis: six 64-electrode Utah arrays (Blackrock Microsystems) per participant, a five-layer gated recurrent unit decoder trained with connectionist temporal classification loss, and a 5-gram language model implemented as a Kaldi weighted finite-state transducer
developer: BrainGate consortium and Neurorecovery, Brown University and VA Providence Healthcare System, with Stanford University and UC Davis co-authors
deployer: BrainGate consortium (BrainGate2 pilot clinical trial; sponsor-investigator Leigh R. Hochberg; FDA Investigational Device Exemption G090003), with research sessions at the participants' residences
segment: People with tetraplegia from ALS or cervical spinal cord injury

ratings.reason: Two identifiable participants typed sentences of their own choosing at up to 22 words per minute. One of them has anarthria and only eye movement left. The typing happened only in research sessions. The paper lists independent use as future work, so the gain is a measurable improvement in a capability.
The outcome is reported for two trial participants in research sessions. A typing rate faster than that of earlier decoders is a research result, and no source reports a realized change for society.

ai_role.statement: The decoder is the component that makes typing possible. It is a recurrent neural network of five gated recurrent unit layers with 512 units each. It was trained with CTC loss on 20 ms bins of threshold crossings and spike-band power. It maps attempted finger movements to characters, and a 5-gram language model corrects them. Without it the arrays only record. The error rate figures are word error rates after the language model. Performance figures come from the developers' own peer-reviewed paper. The paper declares that the MGH Translational Research Center has research support agreements with several BCI companies, for which L.R.H. provides consultative input.

produced_by: Six 64-electrode Utah arrays per participant placed in precentral gyrus after fMRI-guided parcellation, giving hand-motor electrodes for both hands.
A recurrent neural network decoder trained with CTC loss on attempted finger movements, recalibrated from as few as 30 sentences, plus a 5-gram language model.
A keyboard setup the participants already knew. Neither was a touch typist, and both learned the layout over sessions.
A pilot-trial infrastructure that brings research staff and equipment to the participant's residence.
must_hold: Use was confined to research sessions. The paper describes independent use through online decoder training as future work.
Performance differed by participant. T18 reached 22 words per minute with word error below 7% across blocks. T17 reached 47 characters per minute with word error mostly below 15%.
Invasive surgery is required. The device is investigational under an FDA investigational device exemption. The paper reports no clinical-trial safety outcomes.

fields.summary: A BrainGate2 implant with a recurrent neural network decoder turned two paralyzed men's attempted finger movements into typing, at up to 22 words per minute with a 1.6% word error rate.
fields.account: T17 and T18 took part in the BrainGate2 pilot trial (NCT00912041). T17 is a 33-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, tetraplegia and anarthria. He depends on a ventilator. T18 is a 48-year-old man who had a cervical spinal cord injury, graded C4 ASIA A, about 18 months before enrollment. Each received six 64-electrode Utah arrays in precentral gyrus. A decoder of five gated recurrent unit layers, with a 5-gram language model, turned attempted finger movements into QWERTY keystrokes. It needed as few as 30 calibration sentences. Research sessions took place at each participant's place of residence, on trial days 44 to 144. T18 reached 110 characters (22 words) per minute with a 1.6% word error rate. T17 reached 47 characters per minute. Both typed sentences of their own choosing. The paper describes independent use as future work. The work was published in Nature Neuroscience on 16 March 2026. On 30 March 2026 the same team reported in Cell Reports that decoding of attempted speech in T17 was not accurate enough for effective communication. The authors write that they provided communication to T17 through the QWERTY typing interface.
